title: The director and the critic: how to make AI improve its own work
description: Separating who creates from who evaluates changes the result. The critique rounds of the Clint carousel, the scorecard, the contact sheet and the skill that ties it all together.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: Aura and the agents that appear in this tutorial's carousel.

blocks.text: Have you ever proofread your own text and found no mistakes, and then someone else read it and found three in the first line? The same thing happens with AI. When it creates and evaluates in the same breath, it tends to like what it made.

The fix that worked for me was splitting the roles: a director who creates and a critic who evaluates against a fixed yardstick. This is the last tutorial in the series and it closes the loop. Shall we?
The director creates, the critic measures

In practice, it's the same AI at two different moments. In the first, it gets the storyboard and creates. In the second, it gets only the result and a criteria sheet, and has to give a score. The rule is simple: any score below 8 goes back to the director, with the reason written down.
The contact sheet

The critic doesn't watch the video. It looks at a sheet with one frame per beat, side by side. Video fools you: motion distracts and you miss the cut-off text that shows up for half a second. On the sheet, the defect sits still, waiting for you.

There's also a test no eye does well: comparing the last frame with the first, pixel by pixel. If the average difference goes above 1 on a 0 to 255 scale, the loop jolts. This test runs on its own on every render.
The scorecard
Six criteria, from 1 to 10, per slide: hook in frame 0, readability on a phone, smoothness, weight, sound sync and loop. This is the real scorecard from one of the rounds of the Clint carousel.

The two 7s tell an interesting story. The problem wasn't the animation. It was the text inside the real product screenshots, too small on a phone. No motion tweak could fix it. The way out was to redesign those slides with native, bigger elements: the glass phone on slide 2 and the Aura panel on slide 5.
When the critic is you

The scorecard catches what's measurable. What isn't measurable is still on you. With almost every score at 8 or above, I looked at the carousel and said it was missing Clint's personality. No scorecard would have caught that. AI is a great critic of rules. Taste and brand still need a human looking.

That's why the process has a mandatory stop before rendering and another after each round. I approve, ask for tweaks or change direction. Those stops are what brought the phone, the hero lighting and the Aura symbol into the carousel.
The skill that ties it all together

This whole process is packaged in a skill for Claude, criador-de-carrosseis-simples, published by Felipe Borges. A skill is a bundle of instructions and references that Claude loads when the task calls for it. This one carries the carousel strategy, the six-position structure, the critique scorecard and the path to the live version, the same one we saw in this series: HTML with seek(t), Playwright and ffmpeg.

The skill's copy and design grammar was distilled from Alex's carousels (@growithalex). It carries the grammar, not the content. It's the same principle as the previous tutorial: reference without copying.
The loop in five steps
The director creates from the storyboard.
The render produces the video and the contact sheet, and the loop test runs on its own.
The critic scores with the scorecard and writes the reason for every score below 8.
You look at what the scorecard doesn't measure: brand, tone, taste.
Every defect that repeats becomes a rule in CLAUDE.md.

That's it. Six tutorials, one carousel, and the lesson that stuck with me most: AI doesn't replace direction. It executes really well when someone says clearly what good looks like. So, what's going to be your first live carousel?
Closing the loop: how every defect becomes a rule.
